group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 74-year-old man was evaluated late this morning in the vascular anesthesia assessment suite four days before a scheduled elective open repair of a 6.2-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm discovered on surveillance ultrasound ordered for a pulsatile epigastric mass; the surgical team anticipates a midline transperitoneal incision from xiphoid to pubis, aortic cross-clamp time of approximately 45 minutes, operative duration close to four hours, blood loss in the 700- to 1000-mL range with cell-saver availability, large fluid shifts requiring invasive hemodynamic monitoring, and postoperative admission to the surgical ICU for ventilator weaning, vasopressor titration, and hourly urine output checks. The patient drove himself from his rural home 45 miles away, parked on the second deck of the visitor ramp, ascended one flight of stairs, and walked the 180-meter corridor to registration at an unhurried pace, noting that he routinely mows his half-acre lawn with a self-propelled push mower and climbs the twelve steps to his bedroom twice each evening, though he pauses midway to catch his breath when carrying a laundry basket. Five years ago, following a viral upper-respiratory illness, he was hospitalized for new lower-extremity edema and exertional dyspnea; echocardiography at that admission demonstrated a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 35 % without regional wall-motion abnormalities, and coronary angiography performed to exclude obstructive lesions showed widely patent epicardial vessels. Since then he has followed heart-failure clinic quarterly, remains on carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg every morning, and furosemide 20 mg only when his weight rises more than 1 kg over baseline; he denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, recent unintentional weight gain, or ankle swelling and sleeps on a single pillow. A transthoracic echocardiogram obtained four months ago showed ejection fraction 38 %, normal right-sided pressures, and mild functional mitral regurgitation. Two years prior he experienced abrupt left-hand clumsiness and expressive difficulty while reading the newspaper; symptoms resolved in less than thirty minutes, and neurologic evaluation diagnosed a transient ischemic attack attributed to a small ulcerated plaque at the right carotid bifurcation. Magnetic-resonance angiography at that time revealed no critical stenosis, and duplex surveillance earlier this year again showed maximal internal-carotid narrowing of 45 %; he has had no recurrent focal neurologic events. He has never reported exertional chest tightness, arm or jaw discomfort, or unexplained diaphoresis; a symptom-limited Bruce-protocol treadmill test performed one year ago to a target heart rate of 145 beats/min reached stage III (8 METs) without electrocardiographic ST-segment deviation or arrhythmia. Medical history also includes long-standing essential hypertension first treated in his forties, stage 3b chronic kidney disease attributed to hypertensive nephrosclerosis, hyperlipidemia managed with high-intensity atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and benign prostatic hyperplasia controlled with tamsulosin. He has never been diagnosed with diabetes and takes no glucose-lowering agents. Surgical history is limited to an uncomplicated ventral hernia repair at age 60 under general anesthesia. He quit cigarette smoking 15 years ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks a single can of light beer with Friday dinner, and denies recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a father who died of ruptured thoracic aneurysm at 78 and a sister living with chronic heart failure. Review of systems today is negative for fever, productive cough, claudication, abdominal pain beyond the dull central pulsation that prompted imaging, hematuria, or weight loss. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs obtained in the right arm revealed blood pressure 134/76 mm Hg, regular radial pulse 64 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air, oral temperature 36.6 °C, height 178 cm, weight 88 kg, and body-mass index 27.8 kg/m². He appeared euvolemic and in no distress. Jugular venous contour was flat at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was palpable in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line with a sustained but not displaced quality. Auscultation disclosed a soft S3 consistent with known ventricular dysfunction, an intact S1 and physiologic split S2, and no pathologic murmurs. Lungs were resonant with clear breath sounds throughout. The abdomen was protuberant but soft, the aortic pulsation palpable left of midline, and no tenderness or organomegaly was elicited; prior hernia repair scars were well healed. There was no peripheral edema, and distal pulses were 2+ and symmetrical. Neurologic screening revealed full orientation, normal cranial nerves, 5/5 strength, intact sensation to light touch and vibration, and steady tandem gait. Airway evaluation demonstrated Mallampati class II view, 4-cm inter-incisor distance, 7-cm thyromental distance, and full cervical extension. Laboratory studies drawn one hour before consultation showed hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, white blood cells 6.1 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 2.18 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 33 mL/min/1.73 m²; liver-associated enzymes and international normalized ratio were within reference ranges, and fasting glucose measured 102 mg/dL. Twelve-lead electrocardiography recorded today revealed sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute, PR interval 162 ms, QRS duration 96 ms, left-axis deviation, and nonspecific lateral T-wave flattening unchanged from a tracing obtained six months earlier. Upright postero-anterior chest radiograph displayed a mildly enlarged cardiopericardial silhouette and clear lung fields with an incidental curvilinear calcification in the abdominal aorta correlating with the known aneurysm. The peri-operative plan discussed with the patient includes balanced volatile general anesthesia with epidural placement for postoperative analgesia provided clotting studies remain normal, radial arterial line and pulmonary artery catheter for goal-directed fluid and vasodilator management, avoidance of nephrotoxic contrast and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, continuation of beta-blocker and heart-failure neurohormonal therapy the morning of surgery, pre-induction antibiotic prophylaxis, and initiation of low-dose unfractionated heparin approximately six hours after skin closure if bleeding remains minimal. Sequential compression sleeves will be applied in the operating room, and incentive spirometry with early mobilization will begin on the evening of operative day 0 once extubation criteria are met. After a comprehensive discussion of expected hospital course and potential complications—including myocardial depression, stroke, renal deterioration, lower-extremity ischemia, graft infection, and need for unplanned return to the operating room—the patient verbalized understanding of medication and fasting instructions and expressed willingness to proceed with definitive aneurysm repair.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index assigns one point for each of six preoperative risk factors:
- High-risk surgery: planned open intraperitoneal aortic aneurysm repair qualifies → 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: no documented coronary disease, angina, or positive stress test → 0.
- History of heart failure: prior symptomatic systolic heart failure with current EF 38% counts despite present euvolemia → 1.
- Cerebrovascular disease: prior diagnosed TIA → 1.
- Insulin-treated diabetes: no diabetes or insulin use → 0.
- Preoperative creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: measured 2.18 mg/dL → 1.
Total = 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 4.
Final answer: 4
